posts.caption: I had the whole aisle swept by 7:15 and I was proud of it. Shavings out, fresh bedding in, the muck cart loaded to the top and parked by the door while I went to fill water buckets. I was gone four minutes. When I came back the cart was on its side, the aisle looked like a snow globe, and the pony was standing next to it with one foot lifted like he'd been trying to help it up. There was a shaving on his nose. I swept it all again. He supervised from much closer this time.
posts.first: My first pony used to wait until I'd finished picking out his stall and then walk in and lie down in the exact center, very slowly, with a big sigh. Every morning for six years. I started picking it out last just so I could watch him do it.

posts.caption: Somebody at work asked what I do on weekends, so I pulled up the photo my friend took at the barn last Saturday. Me in my good jacket, the chestnut mare beside me, both of us looking at the camera. Half the office crowded around my desk. Someone said gorgeous, and someone else said it again. I went home and hung the picture on the fridge. It wasn't until Wednesday that I zoomed in and noticed the mare had turned her head at the perfect angle. My hair was full of shavings. I'm keeping the picture up anyway.
posts.first: Years ago a coworker asked if my horse knew my name. I said probably not. The next weekend I called her from the gate and she lifted her head from the far end of the pasture and walked the whole way up. I've never brought it up at work again.

posts.caption: The lesson barn down the road has had the same gray gelding since before the owner's kids could drive. He's taught half the county to ride, me included, at forty-four, after twenty years away. I spent most of that first month pulling on the reins about a full second after he'd already stopped. My instructor never said a word. She'd just nod and say nice halt. I bought a horse of my own the next spring. She does not stop before I ask. Some weeks she doesn't stop after I ask, either.
posts.first: On my last lesson before I bought my own horse, I brought the old gelding a bag of carrots and told him thank you. He ate every one, looked at me for a minute, and walked off to stand by the next nervous adult in a brand new helmet.

posts.theme: the horse budget vs. the spouse
posts.quote: We agreed on a $50 limit for our anniversary. I got him a nice wallet. He went way over and got me forty bales of hay. I cried.
posts.first: The first year we were married my husband bought me a dozen roses for Valentine's Day. The horse ate four of them off the porch railing before I got home. The next year he bought me a mineral block with a red bow on it. We've done it that way ever since.

posts.caption: The barn schedule says the mares come in at five. It's printed on the whiteboard in the feed room in the barn owner's handwriting, underlined twice. Big Red has never once read the whiteboard. At three she walks to the gate and plants herself there. She doesn't call. She doesn't paw. She just looks at the barn, steadily, for two hours, like a very large clock. Most days somebody gives in by four. Yesterday it was the barn owner herself. She said she was early because of the weather. It was seventy degrees and sunny.
posts.first: My old mare figured out that the feed truck came on Thursdays. Every Thursday morning she'd stand at the front fence watching the road and ignore everyone else. If the truck was late she'd stay there until it came. The driver started honking twice when he turned in, just for her.

posts.caption: The radio in the barn died in 2019 and I never replaced it. I didn't notice I'd started humming until my neighbor came by one morning and asked what the song was. I didn't know I'd been doing it. Turns out it's always the same three, all from the car my dad drove when I was ten. Every morning, stall cleaning, wheelbarrow, fresh straw, same three songs. The bay mare stands in the corner with her eyes shut the whole time. I thought she was dozing. I'm not so sure anymore.
posts.first: My grandmother used to sing to her cows while she milked, the same hymn every morning. She swore they let down better for it. When she moved to town, my uncle took over the milking and tried singing too. The cows looked at him like he'd lost his mind.
